sources.title: Wikipedia GeoSearch, Chicago Loop, 1.6 km radius
List of National Historic Landmarks in Illinois

stops.name: Cloud Gate
stops.description: A 110 ton sculpture of welded stainless steel with no visible seams, called the Bean by everyone but its artist, bending the whole Loop skyline into its underside.

stops.name: Crown Fountain
stops.description: Two 50 foot glass brick towers play video portraits of a thousand ordinary Chicagoans, and every few minutes a face purses its lips and spouts water at the children below.

stops.name: Chicago Cultural Center
stops.description: Built in 1897 as the city's first central library, it holds the largest Tiffany stained glass dome in the world and costs nothing to walk into.

stops.name: Chicago Picasso
stops.description: Picasso refused payment for this 50 foot Cor-Ten steel head, which baffled the city when it was unveiled in 1967 and is now the thing children slide down on Daley Plaza.

stops.name: Reliance Building
stops.description: Finished in 1895, its walls are mostly plate glass hung on a steel frame, which makes it the direct ancestor of every glass office tower built since.

stops.name: Marshall Field and Company Building
stops.description: Look up inside for the Tiffany mosaic ceiling and out at the great bronze corner clock, both left over from the era when this was the flagship of Marshall Field's.

stops.name: Chicago Theatre
stops.description: The six story marquee spelling out CHICAGO has been the most photographed sign in the city since this movie palace opened in 1921.

stops.name: Sullivan Center
stops.description: Louis Sullivan wrapped the State and Madison corner in swirling cast iron ornament in 1899, some of the most intricate ironwork on any American storefront.

stops.name: Art Institute of Chicago Building
stops.description: Two bronze lions have guarded these Beaux-Arts steps since 1894, and the museum dresses them in helmets whenever a Chicago team reaches a championship.

stops.name: Auditorium Building
stops.description: Adler and Sullivan packed a hotel, an office block and a 4,000 seat theater into one 1889 granite pile, and the theater still carries an unamplified voice to the back row.

stops.name: Buckingham Fountain
stops.description: Modeled on a fountain at Versailles and built at twice the size, its center jet climbs 150 feet on the hour through the warm months.

stops.name: The Berghoff
stops.description: Open since 1898 and holder of Chicago liquor license number one, it still serves the sauerbraten that kept it alive through Prohibition.

stops.name: Marquette Building
stops.description: Step into the lobby for Tiffany mosaics and bronze reliefs retelling Father Marquette's 1670s expedition through the swamp this city was built on.

stops.name: Monadnock Building
stops.description: The tallest load-bearing masonry building ever raised, its brick walls six feet thick at the sidewalk because nothing else could hold up sixteen floors.

stops.name: Rookery Building
stops.description: The oldest standing high rise in Chicago, from 1888, hiding a glass-roofed light court that Frank Lloyd Wright remodeled in white marble and gold in 1905.

note: Chicago has never been scouted before, so this is a first pass at the densest walkable core the city has. Every stop is inside the Loop, roughly a one mile circuit from Millennium Park down State Street, south to Grant Park, then back west along Adams and Jackson to LaSalle; no stop is more than about a ten minute walk from the next. Addresses came from Wikipedia and NRHP infoboxes and were checked against a map service; ZIPs were looked up per address, and two disagreed with the map service and were settled against the venue's own published address (Millennium Park is 60601, the Art Institute is 60603). Dropped for crowding rather than quality, all verified and available for a future run: Chicago Board of Trade Building (141 W Jackson Blvd), Jay Pritzker Pavilion, Fine Arts Building, Palmer House, Flamingo by Alexander Calder on Federal Plaza, Richard J. Daley Center, Willis Tower. Nothing was dropped for being demolished or closed. Deliberately left out of range: the Old Water Tower, Wrigley Building and Tribune Tower are all north of the river and would stretch the walk past two miles.
